metadata.title: A Synthetic Study of Checklist-Assisted Review

pages.text:
SYNTHETIC DEMO - invented study and numbers for software testing only.

Introduction

A Synthetic Study of Checklist-Assisted Review


Reviewers inspect short reports to identify reporting omissions.

This demonstration examines whether a checklist improves omission detection.

RQ1: Does checklist access increase the number of omissions detected?

The aim was to compare checklist-assisted review with unaided review.

Study Design

Twelve volunteer graduate students were recruited through a campus email.

Participants were randomly assigned to two groups of six in a between-subjects design.

Both groups reviewed the same two-page report for 15 minutes and listed omissions.

The checklist group received a printed checklist; the control group reviewed without it.





                                                                                                     1 / 3

SYNTHETIC DEMO - invented study and numbers for software testing only.

Methods


Participants gave consent, received a two-minute tutorial, completed the task, then
rated confidence.

This synthetic demonstration involved no real human participants.

The interface recorded each submitted omission and its timestamp during the task.

After the task, participants rated confidence on a scale from 1 to 5.

For each participant, duplicate omission labels were removed and remaining labels were
counted.

We compared omission counts between groups using a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test.

Results


Median omission counts were 8 for checklist and 5 for control; U = 5, p = 0.041.

The checklist group detected more omissions than the control group in this task.

shown.

Discussion

The authors interpret this pattern as possible support for structured review aids.

This demonstration illustrates a traceable workflow for evaluating a review checklist.

The small sample and single report limit generalization.
